Messages.Author: Johannes Walch
Messages.Body:


And if you have more than one organizer? If you fix this to one person
the following thing will happen: Since only one person gets the "reward"
there will be suddenly only one person doing all the work. Other people
will think "hey, he gets qualified for it, why should I take over some
of the tasks". What about the national coordinators? They contributed
their work even in regular intervals, what will they think, or the
organizers of the continental championships?

What about countries having multiple (mutually exclusive) qualifiers,
like Spain? How many people will qualify there? One -> very unfair. All
of them? This will force the introduction of more multiple qualifiers
per country, for sure. And I don´t think that´s a good thing for most of
the countries, because it seperates the players base to some extent. It
may work for Spain, it will not for other, but if you allow it there you
can not forbid it for others.

In short: Until now there has been no reward for voluntary work in VTES.
Now there will be a reward but only for some specific people and that is
a really bad situation in my opinion.

Also, the qualification system is there to ensure a high level of play
in the championship. Why should people qualify just because they
organize an event?

--
johannes walch

I can't help but think this is a bad thing. Three arguments:

1) Running a qualifier is hard work, but it doesn't make you a
good player. Qualification should be based on performance alone.

2) The larger qualifiers requires more than one person to run
things. Having one carrot in the stakes might make it more
difficult to get person two, three etc interested in running the
event instead of playing.

3) The organizer will most probably be the local prince. The carrot
will even further detract from the rule that the local prince
should be the local demo-slave rather than the prince-in-command.

I firmly believe that any rewards should first and foremost be
rewards strengthening the local playgroup. Now, I can see why
rewarding hard work in other ways might help indirectly, but why
not make it something other than a ticket to the CC? A sideevent
during the timespan of the CC, like a working-dinner instead? Would
help the initial planning of next years CC.

Sten During

'Cause entry to the CC is something that costs nothing and is actually
a handy reward for running a premier event (i.e. a Qualifier). Given
that the person running the Qualifier can't play, and in most cases, it
will be inconvinient to get to another, non local qualifier. By running
a Qualifier, you are, in many cases, giving up the opportunity to
Qualify yourself. It doesn't strike me as at all unreasonable to hand
out a CC qualification.

-Peter

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
XZealot wrote:
> Where does it say that the organizer can not play in the event? I see
> a bunch of people who have made this assumption and I cannot find where
> it is listed.

Tournament Rules, section 2.9 Multi Judge System:

"The Multi-Judge System may be used at any non-qualifier,
non-championship tournament with at least eight participants (i.e.,
having at least two tables). Organizers choosing this system must
announce its use before the tournament begins and identify six judges
as head judge, secondary judge, and third, fourth, fifth, and sixth
judge. Organizers should use good judgement when selecting the
Multi-Judge System and should ensure its use will not disrupt the
event. Tournament organizers may only participate in events they
sanction if they are using the Multi-Judge System. These types of
events are the only ones in which judges and/or tournament organizers
are allowed to participate."

By "Organizer", I suspect that this benefit (i.e. auto-qualification)
refers to "Guy who doesn't play the event, and instead judges the
event".

-Peter

I guess this seems like something that's a bit "self-apparent" to me.
Sten thinks (I'm guessing) that if you're going to tell people they can't
play in an event unless they've qualified through a certain system that
tests players' abilities through competition, that this should be the
only way that one can qualify. Or at least all qualifiers ought to have
demonstrated ability through one means or another. (Obviously, last
year's CC finalists have demonstrated ability by other means.) It's
just a matter of consistency, I guess.

Myself, I personally don't think it's all that big of a deal and I can
see why they might want to bastardize the system in recognition of the
fact that a lot of the guys who are well-qualified to run a CQ are also
people who would want to qualify themselves and so it solves a practical
problem. (Especially given that it's not all that hard to qualify if you
get the chance, all things considered.) But I can why some might find
it a distasteful compromise of an otherwise purely skill-based system.
Just playing Devil's Advocate. (Or "Sten's Advocate" - don't know if
that's the same... :-) )

Dunno. I've seen events run by non-VTES player store owners. I think that
the judge is the ultimate samaritan who would need to get qualified.
Because, well, I assume that being a Judge at an event really assumes
you are at least as versed in the game as the best players, and your
experience is at least sufficient to judge in-game situations impartially.

If anyone should get qualified at all. Because it is hard to resist Fred's
simple but thoughtful point, that if participation is tied to
qualification, then the qualification should be necessary for everyone.

>>> beliefs is schoolyard/webforum argumentation (if said it enough times,
>>> someone might think its a fact). Care to comment on the already-posted
>>> responses to your assertion, instead?
>> I guess this seems like something that's a bit "self-apparent" to me.
>> Sten thinks (I'm guessing) that if you're going to tell people they can't
>> play in an event unless they've qualified through a certain system that
>> tests players' abilities through competition, that this should be the
>> only way that one can qualify. Or at least all qualifiers ought to have
>> demonstrated ability through one means or another. (Obviously, last
>> year's CC finalists have demonstrated ability by other means.) It's
>> just a matter of consistency, I guess.
>>
> If your Sten-guessing is accurate, then I'll reply to it; The CQ organizers

It is correct.

> are the one (absurdly small) subset of players who are denied their (local)
> oportunity to demonstrate their ability, and this through their own act of
> selflessness. Forcing them to travel to qualify runs contrary to the desire
> to continue to foster volunteerism from the player base. Doing this for the
> bureaucratic purpose of making sure every one has their appropriate
> "paperwork" might be consistent (in one sense), but is also inconsistent in
> that it precludes some players from the opportunity to play for the
> championships.

I disagree. I've traveled to Denmark twice in order to qualify as I'm
not eligible for the Gothenburg qualifier. The last two years have had
me qualifying at the last chance qualifier because I didn't play well
enough to make it in Denmark two years ago and because there simply
wasn't time last year.

So I'm one of those who will benefit 50% from the new rule. 50%? Well
try running a 40 player qualifier alone. We'll flip a coin here I guess.

The local prince it NOT a Prince. Prince == Demo Monkey, Card Slave etc.
The thing about NOT receiving an extra benefit is that it makes it
EASIER, not harder, to conscript additional slave-labour for an event,
which what non-profit events are all about.

>
> If the desire for all players to be qualified stems from some desire for a
> de facto standard of player quality in the event, the impact of CQ-qualified
> peoples will be negligible, even without the recently added extra round of
> elimination (assuming that they are even below the standard of a normally
> qualified player. As I said before, I believe there's a case to be made
> that nearly all CQ organizers are also players who are competent enough to
> qualify, if given the opportunity).

I agree that it will be neglible, but it won't SEEM neglible for
all participants.

I'm right on the limit I'd say, but then again, who could fail to
qualify with !Tor/breed/vote/bleed or DOM/bleed/bounce.
I never had to be competent to qualify during the last qualifier
with those decks. An automation would have done as well.

> Yeah, I hear ya, Fred... Unfortunately, we cannot accomdate all players
> when the organizational structure is based on volunteerism. The volunteer
> is always excluded. The current system mitigates this for the tournaments
> which matter most. IMO, its a better compromise... until the game can fund
> its own (corrupt) International VTES Committe, that is ;-)
>

I've already stated my response on volunteerism, and believe me, I have
quite extensive experience in that area.

We have an International VTES Committee already, albeit not corrupt.

Sten During
